# Use TypeScript for the app and server

> **Decision:** Use TypeScript everywhere. **Because** the team already writes it and the Next.js starter uses it. **Accepted cost:** a build step and type errors to fix before shipping. **Revisit if** the team moves to another language.

## Context and Problem Statement
Which language should fieldnotes be written in?

## Decision Drivers
- The team writes TypeScript every day (your answer)
- Next.js starter (seen in package.json)

## Considered Options
1. TypeScript
2. JavaScript

## Decision Outcome
Chosen: TypeScript, because the team already writes it and errors show up before users see them.

### Consequences
- Good, because type errors show up before users see them.
- Bad, because there is a build step to keep working.

## More Information
- Confidence: high; every driver is seen in the repo or answered.

# Host the app on Vercel

> **Decision:** Host on Vercel. **Because** it deploys a Next.js app on every push with nothing to run. **Accepted cost:** functions don't keep files, and costs grow with traffic. **Revisit if** the app needs long-running jobs or a disk.

## Context and Problem Statement
Where should fieldnotes run?

## Decision Drivers
- Nobody wants to run servers (your answer)
- vercel.json in the repo (seen)

## Considered Options
1. Vercel
2. A container on Fly.io

## Decision Outcome
Chosen: Vercel, because it deploys on every push with nothing to run.

### Consequences
- Good, because previews come with every pull request.
- Bad, because functions don't keep files between requests.
- Bad, because costs grow with traffic.

## More Information
- Confidence: high.

plan.task_summary: Add user accounts with saved projects to a minimal Express app (Fieldnotes) deployed on Vercel - requires auth, persistence, and project ownership design from scratch.

profile.text: Who will use this? Just you, a small team, or public users on the internet?
profile.why: Determines if projects need to be private, shared, and how robust auth needs to be.

profile.text: What should logging in feel like for your users?
profile.why: Tradeoff between security, convenience, and implementation complexity for account creation.
profile.beginner_note: OAuth means 'Login with Google/GitHub' - no password to remember.
answers: As frictionless as possible - no passwords
Most secure possible, even if slower

profile.text: What are your constraints for hosting data and costs?
profile.why: Vercel is serverless - choice of database affects cost, vendor lock-in, and latency.
profile.beginner_note: Serverless databases like Vercel Postgres, Turso, or Supabase work well on Vercel; self-hosted Postgres does not.
answers: Stay free/cheap and inside Vercel ecosystem
I have a preferred DB/provider already
Minimize vendor lock-in, keep it portable

profile.text: How important are saved projects long-term?
profile.why: Affects backup, account deletion policy, and how strictly we version project data.
answers: Ephemeral - okay to lose if account deleted
Important - users expect them to persist for years
Critical - like user documents that need export/backup

decisions.title: Choose persistence layer for users and saved projects
decisions.scope: What database/service stores user accounts and project JSON/blobs, and how it's deployed on Vercel. Does not cover auth method or schema details.
decisions.default: Vercel Postgres or Vercel KV with Prisma
decisions.why: Switching databases later requires data migration and rewriting all account/project queries.

decisions.title: Select authentication mechanism
decisions.scope: How users sign up and prove identity - password, magic link, OAuth provider, or third-party auth service. Excludes session token format.
decisions.default: OAuth via Auth.js for Google + GitHub, no passwords
decisions.why: Password handling brings major security liability; changing auth method invalidates existing users and UX.

decisions.title: Define session and token handling
decisions.scope: Whether auth is stateful session cookies vs JWT, cookie security settings, and expiration/refresh logic for Vercel serverless functions.
decisions.default: HttpOnly secure cookie sessions with 30-day expiry
decisions.why: Impacts security, ability to scale on Vercel edge functions, and logout-all-devices capability.

decisions.title: Set project ownership and sharing model
decisions.scope: Whether projects are private per user, public by default, or shareable, and if ownership is single-user or team-based. Covers data model for user->projects relation.
decisions.default: Private to owner by default, with optional public link
decisions.why: Changing from single-owner to shared/team model later requires rewriting permission checks across the app.

decisions.title: Decide account recovery and deletion policy
decisions.scope: How password reset/recovery works, data retention after deletion, and GDPR-style export/delete behavior for saved projects.
decisions.default: Email recovery and soft-delete with 30-day purge
decisions.why: Deletion policy is legally binding once users sign up; retroactively changing it risks data loss or compliance issues.
decisions.budget_note: over the 3-question budget; default recorded for review

options.name: Vercel Postgres (Neon) with Prisma/Drizzle
options.summary: Managed Postgres inside Vercel for users and project JSON.

good.text: One click setup in Vercel dashboard, works with serverless functions
No DB ops, auto-scaling and backups handled

bad.text: Locks you to Vercel/Neon pricing
Migrating away means Postgres dump and import

learn.what: Vercel Postgres is managed Postgres powered by Neon. You connect from your Express/API routes with a connection string and an ORM.
learn.living_with: You add a POSTGRES_URL env var in Vercel. Deploys get DB access automatically, you manage schema via migrations.

terms.meaning: Serverless Postgres provider that Vercel resells as Vercel Postgres
Library like Prisma or Drizzle that maps tables to code

options.check_current: Confirm Vercel Postgres pricing and free tier limits are still listed as Neon-based on Vercel docs.

options.name: Supabase Postgres
options.summary: External managed Postgres with built-in Auth/storage, used via connection string.

good.text: Generous free tier, includes dashboard and backups
Portable Postgres you can self-host if you leave Vercel

bad.text: Second vendor/dashboard to manage alongside Vercel
Extra network hop from Vercel functions can add latency

learn.what: Supabase is hosted Postgres with extra tools. You can use just the database part from Vercel via a Postgres URL.
learn.living_with: You keep Supabase project for DB, set its URL in Vercel env vars. You use Supabase SQL editor for ops.

terms.meaning: Platform that hosts Postgres and adds auth/storage/tools
Reusing DB connections so serverless functions don't exhaust the DB

options.check_current: Confirm Supabase free project limits and connection string pooling (PgBouncer) format before relying on it.

options.name: Turso (libSQL / SQLite) over HTTP
options.summary: Distributed SQLite accessed over HTTP, works well on edge/serverless.

good.text: Very cheap, fast for reads, simple file-based mental model
DB file is portable, easy to backup or move vendors

bad.text: SQLite has fewer Postgres features and different constraints
JSON querying and relational features are weaker for growing project data

learn.what: Turso is SQLite (libSQL) hosted at the edge and queried via HTTP. You get a database URL and auth token.
learn.living_with: You add TURSO_DATABASE_URL and token as env vars. Migrations are SQLite SQL, tooling is lighter.

terms.meaning: Fork of SQLite made for HTTP replication
Single-file relational database, simpler than Postgres

options.check_current: Confirm Turso free tier row/storage limits and HTTP client support still applies.

user-data-store.default_reason: Defaults to cheapest path inside Vercel with no extra vendor and works with serverless.

options.name: OAuth with Google and GitHub
options.summary: Let users sign in via existing Google or GitHub account.

good.text: No passwords to store or hash yourself
Less reset support; users keep security with their provider

bad.text: Need to register OAuth apps and handle provider callbacks
If user loses provider account they lose access unless linked

learn.what: OAuth is a standard where your app redirects to Google/GitHub. They confirm the user and return an ID token. You trust that token as proof of identity.
learn.living_with: You keep a user row with provider ID and email. Login is a redirect flow. You add a second provider by adding another OAuth client.

terms.meaning: Protocol to login via another service without sharing password

options.name: Passwordless magic link via email
options.summary: User enters email, gets a one-time link that logs them in.

good.text: Low friction, no passwords to implement or store
Easy to add secondary factor later without breaking flow

bad.text: Requires working email delivery on Vercel functions
Login fails if email is delayed or in spam

learn.what: On sign-up you create a short-lived token, store its hash, and email a link containing it. Clicking the link sets the session cookie if the token matches.
learn.living_with: You monitor email deliverability and token expiry. Users login same way every time. No password reset flow needed.

terms.meaning: One-time URL sent by email that logs user in when clicked
Random string valid once for a few minutes

options.name: Self-built email and password
options.summary: Classic sign-up with email, password hash stored in your DB.

good.text: Works without any external provider or email delivery for login
Fully portable, no provider lock-in

bad.text: You must correctly hash, salt, and protect passwords
You own password reset, breach handling, and MFA if needed later

learn.what: User submits email and password. Server hashes password with a slow hash like bcrypt and stores hash. On login, hash input and compare to stored hash.
learn.living_with: You enforce password rules and build reset-by-email. You watch for weak passwords and reuse. Each login is local to your code.

terms.meaning: One-way scrambled version of password stored instead of plain text
Common slow hashing algorithm for passwords

options.name: Managed auth service (Clerk, Auth0, Supabase Auth)
options.summary: Offload sign-up, login, and password handling to an external auth service.

good.text: Gets OAuth, magic link, MFA out of the box with SDKs

bad.text: Adds vendor, extra env keys, and pricing to track

learn.what: You install provider SDK in Express and configure it. The service hosts login pages or provides UI components and returns a verified user to your app.
learn.living_with: You manage users in provider dashboard plus your DB. You follow their breaking changes and billing. Day-to-day login is their flow, not yours.

terms.meaning: Third-party service that runs authentication for you

options.name: Private, single-owner
options.summary: Each project has one owner user, private to them only.

good.text: Simplest data model: user_id foreign key on projects

bad.text: No way to share a project even if you want to later

terms.meaning: Column that stores which user owns the row

options.name: Private with shareable links

good.text: Still private by default, but allows collaboration

bad.text: Needs extra table for shares and token handling
You must handle revoking links and permission levels

learn.what: Projects still have one owner_id, plus a project_shares table with project_id, shared_user_id or token, and role like viewer or editor.
learn.living_with: You check owner or a valid share on reads. You need UI to create and revoke links. Ownership stays clear.

terms.meaning: Extra table that records who else can access a project

options.name: Team workspace ownership
options.summary: Projects belong to a team/workspace, all members of the team can access them.

good.text: Good for small teams working on same set of projects
Easy to add new members, they see all team projects

bad.text: Most complex model: needs teams, memberships, and projects tables

learn.what: You have teams, team_members, and projects with team_id instead of user_id. Access is via team membership.
learn.living_with: Every project query goes through team membership check. You maintain invite, role, and leave-team flows.

terms.meaning: A group that owns projects together, also called team or org
Join table linking users to teams

options.name: Public by default
options.summary: Projects are visible to anyone unless marked private.

good.text: Easy discovery and sharing, no share links needed
Can build public gallery or feed without extra sharing logic

bad.text: Privacy risk if users expect projects to be private

learn.what: Projects have a visibility flag public or private. List queries can return all public projects. No ownership check for reading public ones.
learn.living_with: You need to be careful to default to private in UI and enforce filtering. User deletion may need to keep public copies.

terms.meaning: Column that marks if a project is public or private
